actions.body:
Research into autonomous systems reveals that traditional, externally-defined task paradigms are insufficient for unpredictable, real-world environments. Instead, achieving true autonomy requires the capacity for self-generated goals. The GOAL-Robots project framework [source-95fe466131c64554] demonstrates that systems capable of internal goal-setting can expedite the acquisition of flexible skills without human intervention. Similarly, the iCog initiative suggests that mimicking biological cognition—through continuous, embodied, and experience-dependent learning—allows knowledge to emerge from distributed interactions rather than static parameter sets [source-2561135a17314579]. Practical implementation of these systems faces hurdles, specifically in the integration of specialized sub-agent orchestration wrappers and the management of local discovery roots [source-ddf6ac46620a4e24, source-e89086fb744c4b28]. These findings suggest that intelligence, in the context of problem identification, is inextricably linked to the ability to maintain 'always-on' structural plasticity, enabling the system to define its own research frontier.

Summary
To identify and investigate problems without human assignment, an intelligent system must be able to create its own goals and learn continuously from its experiences. Current research suggests this requires moving away from static, predefined instructions toward 'hybrid' architectures that can update their own internal states based on real-world interactions.
actions.lede: Can an artificial system transition from task execution to problem discovery? We examine how hybrid cognitive architectures facilitate self-generated goal acquisition.
